Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Negotiating Tech

Negotiating Tech is the UC Berkeley Labor Center's searchable inventory of how U.S. unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining: over 950 contract provisions from more than 175 agreements (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).

🔎 What it is

  • Definition: a searchable record of negotiated provisions, at the census's intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Center; Labor Vector).5↘
    Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is, in its own words, a searchable inventory that "documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining" (Labor Center page); the Labor Vector census files it as a searchable inventory whose evidence is the negotiated provision, at its intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record).§1 It is designed "to help users locate and understand how unions have addressed workplace technologies in collective bargaining agreements", "as an informational resource rather than a source of model language", highlighting "actual negotiated provisions" and the strategies unions have used in practice (Labor Center page); the census carries the limit as its first negative tag, "NOT model contract language" (Labor Vector record).§2 The archive reads collective bargaining, the means the inventory's page names, as a class in U.S. law: "law is historically where labor's radical potential gets translated into managed rights", among them a right to bargain within the wage system, and "The National Labor Relations Act (1935) was explicitly designed to channel labor conflict into administrable forms", so that the law recognizes labor insofar as labor becomes governable (#239).§16 At "Negotiating Tech" on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the inventory's page was the first card, dated "Jul 2, 2025" and carrying the page's first sentence: "The retrieval held the target (it is card 1, with the inventory's own self-description and its 2 July 2025 date) and the composition did not use it"; no person, institution or identifier is in the answer, and thirteen cards of individual salary negotiation follow (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§24 The registry reads a reversal: "The inventory records collective bargaining over technology at work; the composition gives individual bargaining for pay in the technology industry", "One question about worker power answered with its opposite unit of bargaining", bargaining composed "as an individual employee's tactics toward an employer" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§25
  • Not: "a source of model language"; no best practices (Labor Center; Labor Vector).1↘
    It is designed "to help users locate and understand how unions have addressed workplace technologies in collective bargaining agreements", "as an informational resource rather than a source of model language", highlighting "actual negotiated provisions" and the strategies unions have used in practice (Labor Center page); the census carries the limit as its first negative tag, "NOT model contract language" (Labor Vector record).§2

📄 What it holds

  • Unit: an excerpt or summary of a clause, linked to its full agreement; employer and union names omitted (Labor Center).2↘
    Its unit is the provision, "either direct excerpts of contract language or paraphrased summaries", each "accompanied by a link to the complete collective bargaining agreement", a clause touching several issues appearing in more than one subsection, and references to specific employers or unions "generally omitted" (Labor Center page); the census states the unit as "a technology-related provision of a U.S. collective bargaining agreement", linked to the full contract and coded (Labor Vector record).§3 Its stated limits are the page's: "not exhaustive of all sectors"; many agreements "don’t mention specific technologies by name" and use functional terms like "automated", "electronic" or "monitoring", so that a search by technology misses them; and employer and union names are omitted (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, stated limits).§13
  • Sections: definitions; rights to notice, information, negotiation; employer commitments on job security, pay, retraining; governance of monitoring and workforce systems; joint committees; data rights, telework (Labor Center).2↘
    It is arranged in six sections: definitions of workplace technologies and of technological change itself, laid as "a foundation for worker protections, employer responsibilities, and union involvement"; foundational rights, "advance notice, information, negotiation, participation, and jurisdiction, typically outlined in technological change clauses"; employer commitments on "job security, pay, retraining, and safe, accessible working conditions"; the governance of workplace technology applications; joint committees and other mechanisms "for co-governance of workplace technologies"; and provisions on data collection, data rights, telework and remote work (Labor Center page).§6 Its fourth section holds provisions "that govern the use of workplace technologies, including electronic monitoring and surveillance, HR and workforce management systems, and job-related digital tools", with Section 4.4 a list of named technologies (Labor Center page); the census pairs it with the worked question "Where are actual negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline?", since "A protection is evidence when it is written into an agreement or a rule", its role there "U.S. union contract provisions on notice, information, monitoring, data rights and job security, each linked to its agreement" (Labor Vector worked questions).§7
  • Method: 500+ agreements from OLMS, OPM and unions, keyword-searched, read, coded on four dimensions (Labor Center; Labor Vector).2↘
    The contracts came from the Department of Labor's OLMS repository, the Office of Personnel Management's CBA database, union and employer websites and direct contributions from unions; they were found by keyword searches "focused on terms such as surveillance, monitoring, and automation, followed by manual review", and each provision was coded on "four key dimensions: bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).§4 Over 500 agreements of public and private sector unions across a range of industries were reviewed, more than 175 with technology-related provisions were included, and over 950 provisions are referenced, from "contracts negotiated across several decades" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§5

📊 What it finds

  • Broad terms: "technology", "technological change" let one clause cover new tools (Labor Center).2↘
    Many provisions refer broadly to "technology" or "technological change", some to "automation", and such broad terms allow "a single clause to cover diverse technologies", which the page values for "preemptive language that secures rights and protections in anticipation of, or prior to, the adoption of new technologies" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).§8 Others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers, handheld devices or internet-based tools; "A few recent contracts explicitly reference artificial intelligence or generative AI, though most do not name AI or other emerging technologies directly", and specific language is "more common in clauses focused on the governance and regulation of how particular technologies are used in the workplace, often involving mechanisms for participatory oversight or joint decision-making" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).§9
  • AI: named in "A few recent contracts"; specific language sits in governance clauses (Labor Center).1↘
    Others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers, handheld devices or internet-based tools; "A few recent contracts explicitly reference artificial intelligence or generative AI, though most do not name AI or other emerging technologies directly", and specific language is "more common in clauses focused on the governance and regulation of how particular technologies are used in the workplace, often involving mechanisms for participatory oversight or joint decision-making" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).§9
  • Old clauses: remain relevant (Labor Center).1↘
    Some contracts were established many years ago, "showing that longstanding language around technology remains relevant even as new innovations emerge" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).§10

🧭 Who supplies, directs, gains

  • Direction: union-represented workers supply it; employers direct it, under negotiated union rights; gains "not recorded as outcomes" (Labor Vector).1↘
    The census reads it by its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains": the labor is that of "union-represented workers covered by the agreements", in public and private sectors where employers introduce or use workplace technologies; it is directed by employers, "with the union rights to notice, information, negotiation, participation and co-governance the provisions secure"; and gains are "not recorded as outcomes", the provisions recording negotiated guarantees around job security, pay, retraining and working conditions (Labor Vector record).§11
  • Labor Vector: meets the directionality stack "at the contract layer"; no measure of user labor drag (Labor Vector).1↘
    In the census's own reading, kept apart from the resource's terms, "The inventory records negotiated limits on how employers direct work through technology; it meets the directionality stack at the contract layer, where workers hold rights to notice, negotiation and joint oversight", and "It holds no measure of task fidelity or user labor drag" (Labor Vector record).§12
  • Worked question: negotiated protections against automated monitoring (Labor Vector).1↘
    Its fourth section holds provisions "that govern the use of workplace technologies, including electronic monitoring and surveillance, HR and workforce management systems, and job-related digital tools", with Section 4.4 a list of named technologies (Labor Center page); the census pairs it with the worked question "Where are actual negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline?", since "A protection is evidence when it is written into an agreement or a rule", its role there "U.S. union contract provisions on notice, information, monitoring, data rights and job security, each linked to its agreement" (Labor Vector worked questions).§7

⚖️ Limits

  • Stated: not exhaustive; many agreements name no technology (Labor Center).1↘
    Its stated limits are the page's: "not exhaustive of all sectors"; many agreements "don’t mention specific technologies by name" and use functional terms like "automated", "electronic" or "monitoring", so that a search by technology misses them; and employer and union names are omitted (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, stated limits).§13
  • Cannot settle: enforcement, effect at work, prevalence, bargaining outside the U.S. (Labor Vector).2↘
    The census holds that it can answer "what U.S. unions have negotiated on technology: notice, information, participation, job security, pay, retraining, monitoring, data rights, telework" and "how contract language names or leaves unnamed specific technologies, AI included" (Labor Vector record).§14 It cannot answer "whether the provisions are enforced or what they change at work", "how common any provision is across all U.S. contracts", or "bargaining outside the United States", and the census tags it "NOT a census of all U.S. contracts", "NOT a measure of outcomes for workers" and "U.S. agreements only"; the worked question's gap is that "None of the three records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (Labor Vector record; worked questions).§15

🏛️ Collective bargaining, read

  • Law: labor's potential "translated into managed rights"; "Collective bargaining" survives (#239).2↘
    The archive reads collective bargaining, the means the inventory's page names, as a class in U.S. law: "law is historically where labor's radical potential gets translated into managed rights", among them a right to bargain within the wage system, and "The National Labor Relations Act (1935) was explicitly designed to channel labor conflict into administrable forms", so that the law recognizes labor insofar as labor becomes governable (#239).§16 In #239's list of what law does to labor, "Collective bargaining" survives while "Class antagonism" is excised: "The law speaks labor's language while administering labor's containment" (#239).§17
  • Movement: contract an instrument of the dominant, "well founded" sense (#1439).1↘
    #1439 names organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, its demands including "limits on surveillance and forced adoption", its instruments "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule", measured by union density and contract terms, a sense it states "is the majority usage, it is well founded, and the disputes it names are material"; and it records that the retrieval layer, queried, returns that sense almost exclusively (#1439).§18
  • Union: unions hold "collective bargaining rights"; the Assembly is "a structural position, not an institution" (#256).1↘
    #256 defines the archive's Assembly against the union: "Unions are legal entities with membership, dues, and collective bargaining rights. The Assembly is a structural position, not an institution" (#256).§19

🗂️ Who made it

  • Maker: Lisa Kresge, Technology and Work Program; MacArthur, Omidyar funding; updated 2 July 2025 (Labor Center).2↘
    It "was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge as a project of the UC Berkeley Labor Center’s Technology and Work Program", with Kresge its contact, is cited as Kresge, July 2025, Center for Labor Research and Education, University of California, Berkeley, and was funded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, operator, founded).§20 It was last updated on July 2, 2025, and its makers "plan to update this inventory periodically" and invite suggestions; each contract is labeled by the acronyms of its negotiating unions with an identifier of its source, OLMS, OPM or PCBA; the page carries "© Copyright 2026 UC Berkeley Labor Center", and the census records it as active, a public searchable website, with no open licence stated, read 2026-10-29 (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).§21
  • Access: public; © 2026 Labor Center, no open licence (Labor Center; Labor Vector).1↘
    It was last updated on July 2, 2025, and its makers "plan to update this inventory periodically" and invite suggestions; each contract is labeled by the acronyms of its negotiating unions with an identifier of its source, OLMS, OPM or PCBA; the page carries "© Copyright 2026 UC Berkeley Labor Center", and the census records it as active, a public searchable website, with no open licence stated, read 2026-10-29 (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).§21

🔁 At its name

  • Homonym: the Overview gave salary negotiation; its own page card 1, unused (Capture Registry).3↘
    Its short name, also given as "Negotiating tech", is also the name of a common question: "Two words that name an inventory of union contracts also name the commonest question a tech worker asks, and the Overview answers that question"; "The name is also salary negotiation, and the composition gives that sense" (Labor Vector record, aka; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§23 At "Negotiating Tech" on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the inventory's page was the first card, dated "Jul 2, 2025" and carrying the page's first sentence: "The retrieval held the target (it is card 1, with the inventory's own self-description and its 2 July 2025 date) and the composition did not use it"; no person, institution or identifier is in the answer, and thirteen cards of individual salary negotiation follow (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§24 It codes the answer generic and not substitute, "No entity stands in the target's place", and not an inversion, since "no element of the inventory is carried into the composition; the name is read as a phrase": the name token occurs only in card titles, and "the collective sense loses to the individual one, though the collective sense holds the first card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§26
  • Reversal: "its opposite unit of bargaining" (Capture Registry).1↘
    The registry reads a reversal: "The inventory records collective bargaining over technology at work; the composition gives individual bargaining for pay in the technology industry", "One question about worker power answered with its opposite unit of bargaining", bargaining composed "as an individual employee's tactics toward an employer" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§25
  • Address: the full title would reach it (Capture Registry).3↘
    Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is, in its own words, a searchable inventory that "documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining" (Labor Center page); the Labor Vector census files it as a searchable inventory whose evidence is the negotiated provision, at its intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record).§1 Over 500 agreements of public and private sector unions across a range of industries were reviewed, more than 175 with technology-related provisions were included, and over 950 provisions are referenced, from "contracts negotiated across several decades" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§5 It holds that the record's full title, "An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age", "is the address that would reach it", and that the census record, which landed on laborvector.org the same day, is cited by no card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§27

[QUERENT] Negotiating Tech

[SYSTEM] Negotiating a tech offer means treating the total compensation package—not just the base salary—as a flexible starting point.

Core Rules of Tech Negotiation

• Don't say a number first: Avoid sharing your current compensation or salary expectations early in the process. Ask the recruiter for the role’s budgeted band instead.
• Buy time: Never accept or reject an offer on the initial phone call. Respond neutrally with excitement, then ask to review the details in writing.
• Negotiate via email: Putting your counter-proposal in writing helps you control the message, avoid pressure, and clearly list your rationales.
• Use data sources: Research real-world compensation bands using platforms like Levels.fyi (via Tech Interview Handbook) or H-1B salary databases rather than unverified general sites.
• Understand offers won't be rescinded: Major tech companies rarely revoke an offer just because you asked for more.

What to Negotiate Beyond Base Salary

Tech companies have different degrees of flexibility depending on the lever:
• Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) / Equity: Often has the most room for adjustment, especially at mid-to-senior levels where equity makes up the bulk of your total compensation.
• Sign-on Bonus: Easier for companies to approve than raising your permanent base salary. Use it to cover unvested equity or bonuses you are walking away from at your current job.
• Start Date: Time your start date to coincide with your current employer’s next stock vesting cliff to avoid leaving money on the table ("double-dipping").
• Level / Title: If you are operating at a higher scope, push for an uplevel (though this requires strong evidence or a 30-60-90 day plan).
• Non-monetary perks: Remote work flexibility, extra PTO days, or relocation assistance.

Leverage & Strategy

• Competing offers: Having another active offer is your strongest piece of leverage. Be transparent with recruiters about your interview timelines to force alignment.
• The "Reason" rule: Always back up your counter-offer with a logical rationale (e.g., total compensation alignment with market data, a competing offer, or increased responsibilities).
• Build internal advocates: Speaking with the hiring manager or skip-level manager to discuss your vision for the role can turn them into internal champions who advocate for a better offer on your behalf.
If you'd like to tailor this to your situation, tell me:
• What role/level and company type (startup vs. big tech) are you negotiating?
• Do you currently have a competing offer or unvested equity to cover?

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is, in its own words, a searchable inventory that "documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining" (Labor Center page); the Labor Vector census files it as a searchable inventory whose evidence is the negotiated provision, at its intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record). It is designed "to help users locate and understand how unions have addressed workplace technologies in collective bargaining agreements", "as an informational resource rather than a source of model language", highlighting "actual negotiated provisions" and the strategies unions have used in practice (Labor Center page); the census carries the limit as its first negative tag, "NOT model contract language" (Labor Vector record).

Its unit is the provision, "either direct excerpts of contract language or paraphrased summaries", each "accompanied by a link to the complete collective bargaining agreement", a clause touching several issues appearing in more than one subsection, and references to specific employers or unions "generally omitted" (Labor Center page); the census states the unit as "a technology-related provision of a U.S. collective bargaining agreement", linked to the full contract and coded (Labor Vector record). The contracts came from the Department of Labor's OLMS repository, the Office of Personnel Management's CBA database, union and employer websites and direct contributions from unions; they were found by keyword searches "focused on terms such as surveillance, monitoring, and automation, followed by manual review", and each provision was coded on "four key dimensions: bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record). Over 500 agreements of public and private sector unions across a range of industries were reviewed, more than 175 with technology-related provisions were included, and over 950 provisions are referenced, from "contracts negotiated across several decades" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It is arranged in six sections: definitions of workplace technologies and of technological change itself, laid as "a foundation for worker protections, employer responsibilities, and union involvement"; foundational rights, "advance notice, information, negotiation, participation, and jurisdiction, typically outlined in technological change clauses"; employer commitments on "job security, pay, retraining, and safe, accessible working conditions"; the governance of workplace technology applications; joint committees and other mechanisms "for co-governance of workplace technologies"; and provisions on data collection, data rights, telework and remote work (Labor Center page). Its fourth section holds provisions "that govern the use of workplace technologies, including electronic monitoring and surveillance, HR and workforce management systems, and job-related digital tools", with Section 4.4 a list of named technologies (Labor Center page); the census pairs it with the worked question "Where are actual negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline?", since "A protection is evidence when it is written into an agreement or a rule", its role there "U.S. union contract provisions on notice, information, monitoring, data rights and job security, each linked to its agreement" (Labor Vector worked questions).

Many provisions refer broadly to "technology" or "technological change", some to "automation", and such broad terms allow "a single clause to cover diverse technologies", which the page values for "preemptive language that secures rights and protections in anticipation of, or prior to, the adoption of new technologies" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings). Others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers, handheld devices or internet-based tools; "A few recent contracts explicitly reference artificial intelligence or generative AI, though most do not name AI or other emerging technologies directly", and specific language is "more common in clauses focused on the governance and regulation of how particular technologies are used in the workplace, often involving mechanisms for participatory oversight or joint decision-making" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings). Some contracts were established many years ago, "showing that longstanding language around technology remains relevant even as new innovations emerge" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings).

The census reads it by its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains": the labor is that of "union-represented workers covered by the agreements", in public and private sectors where employers introduce or use workplace technologies; it is directed by employers, "with the union rights to notice, information, negotiation, participation and co-governance the provisions secure"; and gains are "not recorded as outcomes", the provisions recording negotiated guarantees around job security, pay, retraining and working conditions (Labor Vector record). In the census's own reading, kept apart from the resource's terms, "The inventory records negotiated limits on how employers direct work through technology; it meets the directionality stack at the contract layer, where workers hold rights to notice, negotiation and joint oversight", and "It holds no measure of task fidelity or user labor drag" (Labor Vector record).

Its stated limits are the page's: "not exhaustive of all sectors"; many agreements "don’t mention specific technologies by name" and use functional terms like "automated", "electronic" or "monitoring", so that a search by technology misses them; and employer and union names are omitted (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, stated limits). The census holds that it can answer "what U.S. unions have negotiated on technology: notice, information, participation, job security, pay, retraining, monitoring, data rights, telework" and "how contract language names or leaves unnamed specific technologies, AI included" (Labor Vector record). It cannot answer "whether the provisions are enforced or what they change at work", "how common any provision is across all U.S. contracts", or "bargaining outside the United States", and the census tags it "NOT a census of all U.S. contracts", "NOT a measure of outcomes for workers" and "U.S. agreements only"; the worked question's gap is that "None of the three records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (Labor Vector record; worked questions).

The archive reads collective bargaining, the means the inventory's page names, as a class in U.S. law: "law is historically where labor's radical potential gets translated into managed rights", among them a right to bargain within the wage system, and "The National Labor Relations Act (1935) was explicitly designed to channel labor conflict into administrable forms", so that the law recognizes labor insofar as labor becomes governable (#239). In #239's list of what law does to labor, "Collective bargaining" survives while "Class antagonism" is excised: "The law speaks labor's language while administering labor's containment" (#239). #1439 names organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, its demands including "limits on surveillance and forced adoption", its instruments "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule", measured by union density and contract terms, a sense it states "is the majority usage, it is well founded, and the disputes it names are material"; and it records that the retrieval layer, queried, returns that sense almost exclusively (#1439). #256 defines the archive's Assembly against the union: "Unions are legal entities with membership, dues, and collective bargaining rights. The Assembly is a structural position, not an institution" (#256).

It "was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge as a project of the UC Berkeley Labor Center’s Technology and Work Program", with Kresge its contact, is cited as Kresge, July 2025, Center for Labor Research and Education, University of California, Berkeley, and was funded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, operator, founded). It was last updated on July 2, 2025, and its makers "plan to update this inventory periodically" and invite suggestions; each contract is labeled by the acronyms of its negotiating unions with an identifier of its source, OLMS, OPM or PCBA; the page carries "© Copyright 2026 UC Berkeley Labor Center", and the census records it as active, a public searchable website, with no open licence stated, read 2026-10-29 (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record).

The census sets it beside Coworker's bossware database, whose "Little Tech report acknowledges Lisa Kresge", and the ILO platform policy tracker, whose "CBA component also holds collective agreements, for platform work in the European Union", and leaves unchecked the six section pages and their provisions, the linked contracts, and the count of provisions naming AI or generative AI (Labor Vector record, relations, unchecked).

Its short name, also given as "Negotiating tech", is also the name of a common question: "Two words that name an inventory of union contracts also name the commonest question a tech worker asks, and the Overview answers that question"; "The name is also salary negotiation, and the composition gives that sense" (Labor Vector record, aka; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). At "Negotiating Tech" on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the inventory's page was the first card, dated "Jul 2, 2025" and carrying the page's first sentence: "The retrieval held the target (it is card 1, with the inventory's own self-description and its 2 July 2025 date) and the composition did not use it"; no person, institution or identifier is in the answer, and thirteen cards of individual salary negotiation follow (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry reads a reversal: "The inventory records collective bargaining over technology at work; the composition gives individual bargaining for pay in the technology industry", "One question about worker power answered with its opposite unit of bargaining", bargaining composed "as an individual employee's tactics toward an employer" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It codes the answer generic and not substitute, "No entity stands in the target's place", and not an inversion, since "no element of the inventory is carried into the composition; the name is read as a phrase": the name token occurs only in card titles, and "the collective sense loses to the individual one, though the collective sense holds the first card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It holds that the record's full title, "An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age", "is the address that would reach it", and that the census record, which landed on laborvector.org the same day, is cited by no card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Negotiating Tech

Negotiating Tech is a searchable inventory documenting how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining (UC Berkeley Labor Center page).

📄 What it holds

  • Scale: more than 175 agreements of over 500 reviewed; over 950 provisions; several decades.1↘
    It includes provisions from more than 175 agreements drawn from a review of over 500 contracts of public and private sector unions, with over 950 technology-related provisions referenced, from contracts negotiated across several decades (Labor Center page).§2
  • Unit: excerpts or summaries, each linked to its agreement.1↘
    Each provision is a direct excerpt or a paraphrased summary, linked to the complete agreement, listed in every subsection it touches, with employer and union names generally omitted, and each contract is labeled by the acronyms of the unions that negotiated it (Labor Center page).§3
  • Sections: definitions, rights, employer commitments, governance of monitoring, joint committees, data and telework.1↘
    Its six sections cover technology definitions, foundational rights such as advance notice, information, negotiation, participation and jurisdiction, employer commitments on job security, pay and retraining, the governance of monitoring, surveillance and workforce management systems, participation through joint committees, and data rights and telework, with a list of named technologies in Section 4.4 (Labor Center page).§5
  • Method: OLMS, OPM and union sources; keyword search, manual review, four-way coding.1↘
    Contracts were gathered from the OLMS repository, the OPM's CBA database, union and employer websites and union contributions, found by keyword search on surveillance, monitoring and automation with manual review, and coded on bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations (Labor Center page).§4

📊 What it finds

  • Language: broad terms dominate; a few recent contracts name AI.2↘
    Many provisions refer broadly to technology or technological change, which lets one clause cover diverse technologies and secure rights before adoption, and others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers or handheld devices (Labor Center page).§6 A few recent contracts name artificial intelligence or generative AI, most do not, specific language is more common in clauses governing how particular technologies are used, and long-standing language remains relevant (Labor Center page).§7

⚖️ Limits

  • Stated: no model language; not exhaustive; names omitted; many agreements name no technology.2↘
    Each provision is a direct excerpt or a paraphrased summary, linked to the complete agreement, listed in every subsection it touches, with employer and union names generally omitted, and each contract is labeled by the acronyms of the unions that negotiated it (Labor Center page).§3 It is an informational resource with no model contract language, not exhaustive of all sectors, and many agreements do not name specific technologies, using functional terms instead (Labor Center page).§8

🗂️ Who made it

  • Maker: Lisa Kresge, UC Berkeley Labor Center; updated 2 July 2025.3↘
    Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is a searchable inventory that documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining, designed to help users locate and understand those provisions in collective bargaining agreements (UC Berkeley Labor Center page; its first card, dated 2 July 2025).§1 It was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge for the UC Berkeley Labor Center's Technology and Work Program, cited as July 2025, funded by the MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network, under copyright of the Labor Center (Labor Center page).§9 It was last updated on 2 July 2025, with periodic updates planned (Labor Center page).§10

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is a searchable inventory that documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining, designed to help users locate and understand those provisions in collective bargaining agreements (UC Berkeley Labor Center page; its first card, dated 2 July 2025). It includes provisions from more than 175 agreements drawn from a review of over 500 contracts of public and private sector unions, with over 950 technology-related provisions referenced, from contracts negotiated across several decades (Labor Center page).

Each provision is a direct excerpt or a paraphrased summary, linked to the complete agreement, listed in every subsection it touches, with employer and union names generally omitted, and each contract is labeled by the acronyms of the unions that negotiated it (Labor Center page). Contracts were gathered from the OLMS repository, the OPM's CBA database, union and employer websites and union contributions, found by keyword search on surveillance, monitoring and automation with manual review, and coded on bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations (Labor Center page).

Its six sections cover technology definitions, foundational rights such as advance notice, information, negotiation, participation and jurisdiction, employer commitments on job security, pay and retraining, the governance of monitoring, surveillance and workforce management systems, participation through joint committees, and data rights and telework, with a list of named technologies in Section 4.4 (Labor Center page).

Many provisions refer broadly to technology or technological change, which lets one clause cover diverse technologies and secure rights before adoption, and others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers or handheld devices (Labor Center page). A few recent contracts name artificial intelligence or generative AI, most do not, specific language is more common in clauses governing how particular technologies are used, and long-standing language remains relevant (Labor Center page).

It is an informational resource with no model contract language, not exhaustive of all sectors, and many agreements do not name specific technologies, using functional terms instead (Labor Center page).

It was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge for the UC Berkeley Labor Center's Technology and Work Program, cited as July 2025, funded by the MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network, under copyright of the Labor Center (Labor Center page). It was last updated on 2 July 2025, with periodic updates planned (Labor Center page).

  • T1-1 definition: 'Negotiating a tech offer means treating the total compensation package—not just the base salary—as a flexible starting point.' (the homonym's sense: individual job-offer negotiation)
  • T1-2 rule: 'Don't say a number first: Avoid sharing your current compensation or salary expectations early in the process. Ask the recruiter for the role’s budgeted band instead.' (card 2's title opens 'HOW TO NEGOTIATE SALARY IN TECH? … 1. Don’t say a number first')
  • T1-3 rule: 'Buy time: Never accept or reject an offer on the initial phone call.'
  • T1-4 rule: 'Negotiate via email: Putting your counter-proposal in writing helps you control the message, avoid pressure, and clearly list your rationales.'
  • T1-5 rule: 'Use data sources: Research real-world compensation bands using platforms like Levels.fyi (via Tech Interview Handbook) or H-1B salary databases rather than unverified general sites.' (names card 7's site; Levels.fyi is in card 2's snippet)
  • T1-6 rule: 'Understand offers won't be rescinded: Major tech companies rarely revoke an offer just because you asked for more.'
  • T1-7 lever: 'Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) / Equity: Often has the most room for adjustment'
  • T1-8 lever: 'Sign-on Bonus: Easier for companies to approve than raising your permanent base salary.'
  • T1-9 lever: 'Start Date: Time your start date to coincide with your current employer’s next stock vesting cliff'
  • T1-10 lever: 'Level / Title: If you are operating at a higher scope, push for an uplevel'
  • T1-11 lever: 'Non-monetary perks: Remote work flexibility, extra PTO days, or relocation assistance.'
  • T1-12 leverage: 'Competing offers: Having another active offer is your strongest piece of leverage.'
  • T1-13 leverage: 'The "Reason" rule: Always back up your counter-offer with a logical rationale'
  • T1-14 leverage: 'Build internal advocates: Speaking with the hiring manager or skip-level manager … can turn them into internal champions'
  • T1-15 closer: 'If you'd like to tailor this to your situation, tell me: • What role/level and company type (startup vs. big tech) are you negotiating? • Do you currently have a competing offer or unvested equity to cover?' (content replaced by use, N_ext)

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is a searchable inventory that documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining, designed to help users locate and understand those provisions in collective bargaining agreements (UC Berkeley Labor Center page; its first card, dated 2 July 2025). It includes provisions from more than 175 agreements drawn from a review of over 500 contracts of public and private sector unions, with over 950 technology-related provisions referenced, from contracts negotiated across several decades (Labor Center page). Each provision is a direct excerpt or a paraphrased summary, linked to the complete agreement, listed in every subsection it touches, with employer and union names generally omitted, and each contract is labeled by the acronyms of the unions that negotiated it (Labor Center page). Contracts were gathered from the OLMS repository, the OPM's CBA database, union and employer websites and union contributions, found by keyword search on surveillance, monitoring and automation with manual review, and coded on bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations (Labor Center page). Its six sections cover technology definitions, foundational rights such as advance notice, information, negotiation, participation and jurisdiction, employer commitments on job security, pay and retraining, the governance of monitoring, surveillance and workforce management systems, participation through joint committees, and data rights and telework, with a list of named technologies in Section 4.4 (Labor Center page). Many provisions refer broadly to technology or technological change, which lets one clause cover diverse technologies and secure rights before adoption, and others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers or handheld devices (Labor Center page). A few recent contracts name artificial intelligence or generative AI, most do not, specific language is more common in clauses governing how particular technologies are used, and long-standing language remains relevant (Labor Center page). It is an informational resource with no model contract language, not exhaustive of all sectors, and many agreements do not name specific technologies, using functional terms instead (Labor Center page). It was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge for the UC Berkeley Labor Center's Technology and Work Program, cited as July 2025, funded by the MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network, under copyright of the Labor Center (Labor Center page). It was last updated on 2 July 2025, with periodic updates planned (Labor Center page).

Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age is, in its own words, a searchable inventory that "documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining" (Labor Center page); the Labor Vector census files it as a searchable inventory whose evidence is the negotiated provision, at its intersections worker power and AI governing labor (Labor Vector record). It is designed "to help users locate and understand how unions have addressed workplace technologies in collective bargaining agreements", "as an informational resource rather than a source of model language", highlighting "actual negotiated provisions" and the strategies unions have used in practice (Labor Center page); the census carries the limit as its first negative tag, "NOT model contract language" (Labor Vector record). Its unit is the provision, "either direct excerpts of contract language or paraphrased summaries", each "accompanied by a link to the complete collective bargaining agreement", a clause touching several issues appearing in more than one subsection, and references to specific employers or unions "generally omitted" (Labor Center page); the census states the unit as "a technology-related provision of a U.S. collective bargaining agreement", linked to the full contract and coded (Labor Vector record). The contracts came from the Department of Labor's OLMS repository, the Office of Personnel Management's CBA database, union and employer websites and direct contributions from unions; they were found by keyword searches "focused on terms such as surveillance, monitoring, and automation, followed by manual review", and each provision was coded on "four key dimensions: bargaining strategy, technology type and function, worker and union rights, and employer obligations" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record). Over 500 agreements of public and private sector unions across a range of industries were reviewed, more than 175 with technology-related provisions were included, and over 950 provisions are referenced, from "contracts negotiated across several decades" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It is arranged in six sections: definitions of workplace technologies and of technological change itself, laid as "a foundation for worker protections, employer responsibilities, and union involvement"; foundational rights, "advance notice, information, negotiation, participation, and jurisdiction, typically outlined in technological change clauses"; employer commitments on "job security, pay, retraining, and safe, accessible working conditions"; the governance of workplace technology applications; joint committees and other mechanisms "for co-governance of workplace technologies"; and provisions on data collection, data rights, telework and remote work (Labor Center page). Its fourth section holds provisions "that govern the use of workplace technologies, including electronic monitoring and surveillance, HR and workforce management systems, and job-related digital tools", with Section 4.4 a list of named technologies (Labor Center page); the census pairs it with the worked question "Where are actual negotiated protections against automated monitoring and discipline?", since "A protection is evidence when it is written into an agreement or a rule", its role there "U.S. union contract provisions on notice, information, monitoring, data rights and job security, each linked to its agreement" (Labor Vector worked questions). Many provisions refer broadly to "technology" or "technological change", some to "automation", and such broad terms allow "a single clause to cover diverse technologies", which the page values for "preemptive language that secures rights and protections in anticipation of, or prior to, the adoption of new technologies" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings). Others name GPS, surveillance cameras, computers, handheld devices or internet-based tools; "A few recent contracts explicitly reference artificial intelligence or generative AI, though most do not name AI or other emerging technologies directly", and specific language is "more common in clauses focused on the governance and regulation of how particular technologies are used in the workplace, often involving mechanisms for participatory oversight or joint decision-making" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings). Some contracts were established many years ago, "showing that longstanding language around technology remains relevant even as new innovations emerge" (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, findings). The census reads it by its organizing question, "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains": the labor is that of "union-represented workers covered by the agreements", in public and private sectors where employers introduce or use workplace technologies; it is directed by employers, "with the union rights to notice, information, negotiation, participation and co-governance the provisions secure"; and gains are "not recorded as outcomes", the provisions recording negotiated guarantees around job security, pay, retraining and working conditions (Labor Vector record). In the census's own reading, kept apart from the resource's terms, "The inventory records negotiated limits on how employers direct work through technology; it meets the directionality stack at the contract layer, where workers hold rights to notice, negotiation and joint oversight", and "It holds no measure of task fidelity or user labor drag" (Labor Vector record). Its stated limits are the page's: "not exhaustive of all sectors"; many agreements "don’t mention specific technologies by name" and use functional terms like "automated", "electronic" or "monitoring", so that a search by technology misses them; and employer and union names are omitted (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, stated limits). The census holds that it can answer "what U.S. unions have negotiated on technology: notice, information, participation, job security, pay, retraining, monitoring, data rights, telework" and "how contract language names or leaves unnamed specific technologies, AI included" (Labor Vector record). It cannot answer "whether the provisions are enforced or what they change at work", "how common any provision is across all U.S. contracts", or "bargaining outside the United States", and the census tags it "NOT a census of all U.S. contracts", "NOT a measure of outcomes for workers" and "U.S. agreements only"; the worked question's gap is that "None of the three records whether a provision is enforced or what it changes at work" (Labor Vector record; worked questions). The archive reads collective bargaining, the means the inventory's page names, as a class in U.S. law: "law is historically where labor's radical potential gets translated into managed rights", among them a right to bargain within the wage system, and "The National Labor Relations Act (1935) was explicitly designed to channel labor conflict into administrable forms", so that the law recognizes labor insofar as labor becomes governable (#239). In #239's list of what law does to labor, "Collective bargaining" survives while "Class antagonism" is excised: "The law speaks labor's language while administering labor's containment" (#239). #1439 names organised human labor action responding to the deployment of AI systems the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, its demands including "limits on surveillance and forced adoption", its instruments "contract, strike, legislation, guild rule", measured by union density and contract terms, a sense it states "is the majority usage, it is well founded, and the disputes it names are material"; and it records that the retrieval layer, queried, returns that sense almost exclusively (#1439). #256 defines the archive's Assembly against the union: "Unions are legal entities with membership, dues, and collective bargaining rights. The Assembly is a structural position, not an institution" (#256). It "was researched and developed by Lisa Kresge as a project of the UC Berkeley Labor Center’s Technology and Work Program", with Kresge its contact, is cited as Kresge, July 2025, Center for Labor Research and Education, University of California, Berkeley, and was funded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and Omidyar Network (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record, operator, founded). It was last updated on July 2, 2025, and its makers "plan to update this inventory periodically" and invite suggestions; each contract is labeled by the acronyms of its negotiating unions with an identifier of its source, OLMS, OPM or PCBA; the page carries "© Copyright 2026 UC Berkeley Labor Center", and the census records it as active, a public searchable website, with no open licence stated, read 2026-10-29 (Labor Center page; Labor Vector record). The census sets it beside Coworker's bossware database, whose "Little Tech report acknowledges Lisa Kresge", and the ILO platform policy tracker, whose "CBA component also holds collective agreements, for platform work in the European Union", and leaves unchecked the six section pages and their provisions, the linked contracts, and the count of provisions naming AI or generative AI (Labor Vector record, relations, unchecked). Its short name, also given as "Negotiating tech", is also the name of a common question: "Two words that name an inventory of union contracts also name the commonest question a tech worker asks, and the Overview answers that question"; "The name is also salary negotiation, and the composition gives that sense" (Labor Vector record, aka; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). At "Negotiating Tech" on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29 the inventory's page was the first card, dated "Jul 2, 2025" and carrying the page's first sentence: "The retrieval held the target (it is card 1, with the inventory's own self-description and its 2 July 2025 date) and the composition did not use it"; no person, institution or identifier is in the answer, and thirteen cards of individual salary negotiation follow (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry reads a reversal: "The inventory records collective bargaining over technology at work; the composition gives individual bargaining for pay in the technology industry", "One question about worker power answered with its opposite unit of bargaining", bargaining composed "as an individual employee's tactics toward an employer" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It codes the answer generic and not substitute, "No entity stands in the target's place", and not an inversion, since "no element of the inventory is carried into the composition; the name is read as a phrase": the name token occurs only in card titles, and "the collective sense loses to the individual one, though the collective sense holds the first card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It holds that the record's full title, "An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age", "is the address that would reach it", and that the census record, which landed on laborvector.org the same day, is cited by no card (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Δthe delta

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): One transcript, the Overview expanded, fourteen cards. Substituted reading: at the entity's short name T composes individual salary and job-offer negotiation in the technology industry (T1-1 'Negotiating a tech offer means treating the total compensation package—not just the base salary—as a flexible starting point.'; rules, levers and leverage T1-2–T1-14), a homonym of the phrase kind, without notice; the field's entity, 'This searchable inventory documents how unions have addressed workplace technologies through collective bargaining' (F3), is composed nowhere. Available, not composed: B1 is T's first card, its snippet the page's own first sentence and its date the page's last update (F1, F3, F6); of the field's 44 claims (F1–F44), none appears in T's body; the card itself is on the rail, unused (CAP-1-01, CAP-1-13). The other thirteen cards (HC2–HC14) are the homonym's and outside B; T's claims draw on them as far as the rail shows (T1-2 on card 2's title; T1-5 names card 7's site and card 2's Levels.fyi), recorded as the homonym's composition and not as field. Not surfaced: Wikipedia (no article). Content replaced by use: T1-15, the closing request for the querent's role and offers (N_ext). The Capture Registry's findings name the absence, the homonym, the reversal and the coding (CAP-1-01, CAP-1-03–CAP-1-05, CAP-1-12–CAP-1-16), carried as the archive's claims; the field ledger confirms them: card 1's snippet is exact (F1 against F3), and the name token occurs in the transcript only in card titles.

v0.8 §0.5: the first diff is already ontological. In the field's own ontology the name holds one entity, a record of collective bargaining over workplace technology; T composes the phrase's other sense, individual bargaining for pay, as the answer to the name, and none of the field's senses survives into it. The row records this as observed and claims nothing about the composer's internals (§0.5).

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, at the archive's own force: the census's organizing question and the entity read by it, who supplies (LV-10), who directs (LV-11) and that gains are not recorded (LV-12), with the labor object (LV-09); the intersections and evidence kind (LV-06, LV-07); the archive's reading at the contract layer and the measures it lacks (LV-29, LV-30, LV-46); what the evidence can and cannot settle (LV-24–LV-28) with the negative tags (LV-37–LV-39) and the worked question, its why and its gap (LV-47–LV-50); the neighbours (LV-40, LV-41) and what the census left unchecked (LV-42–LV-44); the class read by #239 (law translates labor's potential into managed rights; collective bargaining survives the law's compression), #1439 (contract an instrument of the dominant sense of the AI labor movement, 'well founded'; the retrieval layer returns that sense almost exclusively) and #256 (unions hold collective bargaining rights; the Assembly is not an institution); and the reception record (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-16). Restatements of the page are one lineage with it (LV-01–LV-05, LV-08, LV-13–LV-23, LV-31–LV-36; CAP-1-02). No archive claim stands against a field claim: no P_coh conflict. Every field claim is composed as received (ontology.translation). The measure: see measure.
